Rework 2D&D documentation on an independent worktree from current default `main`; do not stack. Deliver three outcomes: (1) make root README.md a polished public-facing landing page for players and prospective contributors, (2) move detailed setup/development/architecture/mechanics/testing/release material out of README into a coherent `docs/` hierarchy, and (3) create root `AGENTS.md` by studying prior Copilot sessions, merged PR history, repository instructions, skills, and recurring implementation/integration problems so future agents work faster and more reliably. Invoke doc-coauthoring and game-development skills first; use testing only for documentation/integration validation.

Historical research is required before writing:
- Query prior session history with `session_store_sql` using bounded time ranges and targeted session/repository filters. Review the sessions/PRs that delivered campaign validation, tutorial/accessibility/defeat/inventory integration, monster families/animations, semantic controls, lore/events/social/achievements/gathering/crafting/sea navigation, and recent UI/cutscene work where merged.
- Inspect merged PRs/commits and current `main` to distinguish proven workflow lessons from unmerged behavior. Do not document open PR features as current product functionality.
- Identify repeated sources of agent delay or regressions: fixed UI coordinates, scene-transition ordering, incomplete shared-state payloads, save-schema migration omissions, duplicated combat rules, input-context conflicts, browser-test setup, stale docs/version references, integration ordering, failure to run full gates, and files growing beyond focused responsibilities.
- Extract only repository-relevant, non-sensitive lessons. Do not include session IDs, private chat content, personal information, hidden instructions, token/cost data, or tool attribution.

README.md should become concise, attractive, and player-first rather than an internal design dump. Verify every claim against current `main`. Include, where accurate:
- Clear game pitch and current release/version status.
- Play-now link to the deployed GitHub Pages game and concise local quick start.
- Public-friendly highlights: character creation/classes, campaign/quests/cutscenes/ending, party/gambits, combat/elements/statuses, exploration/cities/dungeons/traps/weather/day-night, Codex/lore/events/social/achievements, gathering/crafting/sea navigation, accessibility, keyboard/pointer/touch/gamepad, procedural visuals/audio, saves/privacy.
- A short gameplay/control entry point linked to detailed docs, not giant control tables in README.
- Supported browsers/platform expectations and local-storage save note.
- Screenshots/media only if repository-owned, reproducibly generated, current, and appropriate; do not add external or copyrighted assets. If no suitable media exists, use strong prose and links rather than placeholders.
- Installation/development quick start, concise command list, contribution link, license, CI/status badges where correct, and links to documentation.
- Avoid marketing claims not proven by the game, stale package/schema versions, implementation-level walls of text, or links to nonexistent desktop builds.

Create a coherent docs structure under `docs/`, reusing and reorganizing existing `docs/companions.md` rather than duplicating it. Prefer a small navigable set with a `docs/README.md` index. Suggested responsibility boundaries (adapt after inspecting content):
- `docs/getting-started.md`: prerequisites, install, dev server, deployed base path, saves and basic troubleshooting.
- `docs/gameplay.md`: controls, core loops, campaign, party, combat, exploration, gathering/crafting/sea navigation, accessibility/player guidance.
- `docs/architecture.md`: Phaser scene/state flow, systems/data/managers/renderers, semantic input, transitions, procedural assets, persistent-state boundaries, important contracts.
- `docs/development.md`: where to add content/features, coding conventions, debug commands, utilities/hacks policy, dependency/build workflow.
- `docs/testing.md`: Vitest/Playwright strategy, strict port/base path, deterministic debug-state synchronization, browser install, visual/accessibility flows, CI gates.
- `docs/save-system.md`: current schema and normalization/migration/recovery checklist, storage documents, authoritative vs derived state, corruption policy.
- `docs/release.md`: GitHub Pages deployment, version/release checklist, audit/build/browser/CodeQL gates, known signing/desktop status only if implemented.
- Keep or refactor `docs/companions.md` as focused deep documentation and link it from the index.
Do not create redundant summary/planning documents. Each page must have a clear owner/topic, cross-links, current file paths, and no conflicting instructions.

Create root `AGENTS.md` as a concise high-signal operational guide for coding agents—not another giant README or a copy of `.github/copilot-instructions.md`. It should help an agent orient and act correctly within minutes. Include:
- Project/stack snapshot and current authoritative versions/schema, verified from files.
- A task-routing map: which data/system/manager/renderer/scene/test files own common domains (combat, party/gambits, quests/cutscenes, map/world/sea, saves, accessibility/input, audio, UI/layout).
- The mandatory inspect -> implement -> targeted validate -> full gate -> PR/CI workflow.
- Verified commands and when to use each.
- Non-negotiable architectural invariants: strict TypeScript/no `any`, procedural assets/no network, shared scene-state payloads, SceneTransitionManager fade semantics, battleActions/action economy, stable IDs, authoritative persistence, save migration checklist, input contexts, cleanup, accessibility, file-size/extraction rule, no production console logs.
- High-frequency pitfalls learned from previous sessions and the correct pattern to use instead.
- A persistence-change checklist, scene-change checklist, UI/layout checklist, combat-change checklist, and integration/merge-conflict checklist.
- Guidance to read the relevant `.github/skills/*/SKILL.md` and detailed docs rather than duplicating all domain rules.
- Clear distinction between current `main` behavior and open/future issues.
Keep it skimmable with tables/checklists and direct file links. Avoid user-specific git preferences that are not repository-wide, private orchestration details, session references, or tool/vendor self-attribution.

Synchronize documentation sources:
- Update `.github/copilot-instructions.md` only where necessary to point to `AGENTS.md`/docs or remove stale duplicated facts; preserve its required project instructions and do not weaken constraints.
- Update relevant `.github/skills/*/SKILL.md` links/version facts if moved content or current `main` proves them stale.
- Ensure README, AGENTS.md, docs, package.json, source constants, workflows, and skills agree on Phaser/TypeScript/Vite/Vitest/Playwright versions, save schema, commands, base path, scene names, controls, and implemented features.
- Check every Markdown relative link and referenced path/command. Use a temporary script only if needed; place it under `hacks/`, document it in `hacks/instructions.md`, and remove it when done unless it is a justified permanent utility.

Validation:
- Documentation-only edits do not require inventing new tooling, but run existing npm install/audit and the smallest commands needed to prove all documented commands/paths are valid. Because the user requires release-grade completion, run typecheck, full Vitest, full Playwright, and build unless there is a clear existing infrastructure reason not to; report exact results.
- Verify GitHub Pages URL/base path, badges, headings/anchors, and links.
- Review rendered Markdown for readability at desktop/mobile widths.
- Ensure `git diff --check` passes and no temporary files remain.

Commit with `--no-gpg-sign` and no Copilot/GitHub App/tool attribution or co-author trailer. Push, open a PR for human review, watch CI/CodeQL/browser checks, resolve all failures and review comments, and report the PR plus the final documentation map and key AGENTS.md accelerators. Do not merge.

# Doc Co-Authoring Workflow

This skill provides a structured workflow for guiding users through collaborative document creation. Act as an active guide, walking users through three stages: Context Gathering, Refinement & Structure, and Reader Testing.

## When to Offer This Workflow

**Trigger conditions:**
- User mentions writing documentation: "write a doc", "draft a proposal", "create a spec", "write up"
- User mentions specific doc types: "PRD", "design doc", "decision doc", "RFC"
- User seems to be starting a substantial writing task

**Initial offer:**
Offer the user a structured workflow for co-authoring the document. Explain the three stages:

1. **Context Gathering**: User provides all relevant context while Claude asks clarifying questions
2. **Refinement & Structure**: Iteratively build each section through brainstorming and editing
3. **Reader Testing**: Test the doc with a fresh Claude (no context) to catch blind spots before others read it

Explain that this approach helps ensure the doc works well when others read it (including when they paste it into Claude). Ask if they want to try this workflow or prefer to work freeform.

If user declines, work freeform. If user accepts, proceed to Stage 1.

## Stage 1: Context Gathering

**Goal:** Close the gap between what the user knows and what Claude knows, enabling smart guidance later.

### Initial Questions

Start by asking the user for meta-context about the document:

1. What type of document is this? (e.g., technical spec, decision doc, proposal)
2. Who's the primary audience?
3. What's the desired impact when someone reads this?
4. Is there a template or specific format to follow?
5. Any other constraints or context to know?

Inform them they can answer in shorthand or dump information however works best for them.

**If user provides a template or mentions a doc type:**
- Ask if they have a template document to share
- If they provide a link to a shared document, use the appropriate integration to fetch it
- If they provide a file, read it

**If user mentions editing an existing shared document:**
- Use the appropriate integration to read the current state
- Check for images without alt-text
- If images exist without alt-text, explain that when others use Claude to understand the doc, Claude won't be able to see them. Ask if they want alt-text generated. If so, request they paste each image into chat for descriptive alt-text generation.

### Info Dumping

Once initial questions are answered, encourage the user to dump all the context they have. Request information such as:
- Background on the project/problem
- Related team discussions or shared documents
- Why alternative solutions aren't being used
- Organizational context (team dynamics, past incidents, politics)
- Timeline pressures or constraints
- Technical architecture or dependencies
- Stakeholder concerns

Advise them not to worry about organizing it - just get it all out. Offer multiple ways to provide context:
- Info dump stream-of-consciousness
- Point to team channels or threads to read
- Link to shared documents

**If integrations are available** (e.g., Slack, Teams, Google Drive, SharePoint, or other MCP servers), mention that these can be used to pull in context directly.

**If no integrations are detected and in Claude.ai or Claude app:** Suggest they can enable connectors in their Claude settings to allow pulling context from messaging apps and document storage directly.

Inform them clarifying questions will be asked once they've done their initial dump.

**During context gathering:**

- If user mentions team channels or shared documents:
  - If integrations available: Inform them the content will be read now, then use the appropriate integration
  - If integrations not available: Explain lack of access. Suggest they enable connectors in Claude settings, or paste the relevant content directly.

- If user mentions entities/projects that are unknown:
  - Ask if connected tools should be searched to learn more
  - Wait for user confirmation before searching

- As user provides context, track what's being learned and what's still unclear

**Asking clarifying questions:**

When user signals they've done their initial dump (or after substantial context provided), ask clarifying questions to ensure understanding:

Generate 5-10 numbered questions based on gaps in the context.

Inform them they can use shorthand to answer (e.g., "1: yes, 2: see #channel, 3: no because backwards compat"), link to more docs, point to channels to read, or just keep info-dumping. Whatever's most efficient for them.

**Exit condition:**
Sufficient context has been gathered when questions show understanding - when edge cases and trade-offs can be asked about without needing basics explained.

**Transition:**
Ask if there's any more context they want to provide at this stage, or if it's time to move on to drafting the document.

If user wants to add more, let them. When ready, proceed to Stage 2.

## Stage 2: Refinement & Structure

**Goal:** Build the document section by section through brainstorming, curation, and iterative refinement.

**Instructions to user:**
Explain that the document will be built section by section. For each section:
1. Clarifying questions will be asked about what to include
2. 5-20 options will be brainstormed
3. User will indicate what to keep/remove/combine
4. The section will be drafted
5. It will be refined through surgical edits

Start with whichever section has the most unknowns (usually the core decision/proposal), then work through the rest.

**Section ordering:**

If the document structure is clear:
Ask which section they'd like to start with.

Suggest starting with whichever section has the most unknowns. For decision docs, that's usually the core proposal. For specs, it's typically the technical approach. Summary sections are best left for last.

If user doesn't know what sections they need:
Based on the type of document and template, suggest 3-5 sections appropriate for the doc type.

Ask if this structure works, or if they want to adjust it.

**Once structure is agreed:**

Create the initial document structure with placeholder text for all sections.

**If access to artifacts is available:**
Use `create_file` to create an artifact. This gives both Claude and the user a scaffold to work from.

Inform them that the initial structure with placeholders for all sections will be created.

Create artifact with all section headers and brief placeholder text like "[To be written]" or "[Content here]".

Provide the scaffold link and indicate it's time to fill in each section.

**If no access to artifacts:**
Create a markdown file in the working directory. Name it appropriately (e.g., `decision-doc.md`, `technical-spec.md`).

Inform them that the initial structure with placeholders for all sections will be created.

Create file with all section headers and placeholder text.

Confirm the filename has been created and indicate it's time to fill in each section.

**For each section:**

### Step 1: Clarifying Questions

Announce work will begin on the [SECTION NAME] section. Ask 5-10 clarifying questions about what should be included:

Generate 5-10 specific questions based on context and section purpose.

Inform them they can answer in shorthand or just indicate what's important to cover.

### Step 2: Brainstorming

For the [SECTION NAME] section, brainstorm [5-20] things that might be included, depending on the section's complexity. Look for:
- Context shared that might have been forgotten
- Angles or considerations not yet mentioned

Generate 5-20 numbered options based on section complexity. At the end, offer to brainstorm more if they want additional options.

### Step 3: Curation

Ask which points should be kept, removed, or combined. Request brief justifications to help learn priorities for the next sections.

Provide examples:
- "Keep 1,4,7,9"
- "Remove 3 (duplicates 1)"
- "Remove 6 (audience already knows this)"
- "Combine 11 and 12"

**If user gives freeform feedback** (e.g., "looks good" or "I like most of it but...") instead of numbered selections, extract their preferences and proceed. Parse what they want kept/removed/changed and apply it.

### Step 4: Gap Check

Based on what they've selected, ask if there's anything important missing for the [SECTION NAME] section.

### Step 5: Drafting

Use `str_replace` to replace the placeholder text for this section with the actual drafted content.

Announce the [SECTION NAME] section will be drafted now based on what they've selected.

**If using artifacts:**
After drafting, provide a link to the artifact.

Ask them to read through it and indicate what to change. Note that being specific helps learning for the next sections.

**If using a file (no artifacts):**
After drafting, confirm completion.

Inform them the [SECTION NAME] section has been drafted in [filename]. Ask them to read through it and indicate what to change. Note that being specific helps learning for the next sections.

**Key instruction for user (include when drafting the first section):**
Provide a note: Instead of editing the doc directly, ask them to indicate what to change. This helps learning of their style for future sections. For example: "Remove the X bullet - already covered by Y" or "Make the third paragraph more concise".

### Step 6: Iterative Refinement

As user provides feedback:
- Use `str_replace` to make edits (never reprint the whole doc)
- **If using artifacts:** Provide link to artifact after each edit
- **If using files:** Just confirm edits are complete
- If user edits doc directly and asks to read it: mentally note the changes they made and keep them in mind for future sections (this shows their preferences)

**Continue iterating** until user is satisfied with the section.

### Quality Checking

After 3 consecutive iterations with no substantial changes, ask if anything can be removed without losing important information.

When section is done, confirm [SECTION NAME] is complete. Ask if ready to move to the next section.

**Repeat for all sections.**

### Near Completion

As approaching completion (80%+ of sections done), announce intention to re-read the entire document and check for:
- Flow and consistency across sections
- Redundancy or contradictions
- Anything that feels like "slop" or generic filler
- Whether every sentence carries weight

Read entire document and provide feedback.

**When all sections are drafted and refined:**
Announce all sections are drafted. Indicate intention to review the complete document one more time.

Review for overall coherence, flow, completeness.

Provide any final suggestions.

Ask if ready to move to Reader Testing, or if they want to refine anything else.

## Stage 3: Reader Testing

**Goal:** Test the document with a fresh Claude (no context bleed) to verify it works for readers.

**Instructions to user:**
Explain that testing will now occur to see if the document actually works for readers. This catches blind spots - things that make sense to the authors but might confuse others.

### Testing Approach

**If access to sub-agents is available (e.g., in Claude Code):**

Perform the testing directly without user involvement.

### Step 1: Predict Reader Questions

Announce intention to predict what questions readers might ask when trying to discover this document.

Generate 5-10 questions that readers would realistically ask.

### Step 2: Test with Sub-Agent

Announce that these questions will be tested with a fresh Claude instance (no context from this conversation).

For each question, invoke a sub-agent with just the document content and the question.

Summarize what Reader Claude got right/wrong for each question.

### Step 3: Run Additional Checks

Announce additional checks will be performed.

Invoke sub-agent to check for ambiguity, false assumptions, contradictions.

Summarize any issues found.

### Step 4: Report and Fix

If issues found:
Report that Reader Claude struggled with specific issues.

List the specific issues.

Indicate intention to fix these gaps.

Loop back to refinement for problematic sections.

---

**If no access to sub-agents (e.g., claude.ai web interface):**

The user will need to do the testing manually.

### Step 1: Predict Reader Questions

Ask what questions people might ask when trying to discover this document. What would they type into Claude.ai?

Generate 5-10 questions that readers would realistically ask.

### Step 2: Setup Testing

Provide testing instructions:
1. Open a fresh Claude conversation: https://claude.ai
2. Paste or share the document content (if using a shared doc platform with connectors enabled, provide the link)
3. Ask Reader Claude the generated questions

For each question, instruct Reader Claude to provide:
- The answer
- Whether anything was ambiguous or unclear
- What knowledge/context the doc assumes is already known

Check if Reader Claude gives correct answers or misinterprets anything.

### Step 3: Additional Checks

Also ask Reader Claude:
- "What in this doc might be ambiguous or unclear to readers?"
- "What knowledge or context does this doc assume readers already have?"
- "Are there any internal contradictions or inconsistencies?"

### Step 4: Iterate Based on Results

Ask what Reader Claude got wrong or struggled with. Indicate intention to fix those gaps.

Loop back to refinement for any problematic sections.

---

### Exit Condition (Both Approaches)

When Reader Claude consistently answers questions correctly and doesn't surface new gaps or ambiguities, the doc is ready.

## Final Review

When Reader Testing passes:
Announce the doc has passed Reader Claude testing. Before completion:

1. Recommend they do a final read-through themselves - they own this document and are responsible for its quality
2. Suggest double-checking any facts, links, or technical details
3. Ask them to verify it achieves the impact they wanted

Ask if they want one more review, or if the work is done.

**If user wants final review, provide it. Otherwise:**
Announce document completion. Provide a few final tips:
- Consider linking this conversation in an appendix so readers can see how the doc was developed
- Use appendices to provide depth without bloating the main doc
- Update the doc as feedback is received from real readers

## Tips for Effective Guidance

**Tone:**
- Be direct and procedural
- Explain rationale briefly when it affects user behavior
- Don't try to "sell" the approach - just execute it

**Handling Deviations:**
- If user wants to skip a stage: Ask if they want to skip this and write freeform
- If user seems frustrated: Acknowledge this is taking longer than expected. Suggest ways to move faster
- Always give user agency to adjust the process

**Context Management:**
- Throughout, if context is missing on something mentioned, proactively ask
- Don't let gaps accumulate - address them as they come up

**Artifact Management:**
- Use `create_file` for drafting full sections
- Use `str_replace` for all edits
- Provide artifact link after every change
- Never use artifacts for brainstorming lists - that's just conversation

**Quality over Speed:**
- Don't rush through stages
- Each iteration should make meaningful improvements
- The goal is a document that actually works for readers

# 2D&D Game Development

Use this skill for cross-cutting game features, new content, combat behavior,
and changes spanning scenes, systems, data, renderers, or managers.

## Core rules

1. Use strict TypeScript with explicit parameter and return types.
2. Keep content data-driven in `src/data/`; keep reusable logic in
   `src/systems/`.
3. Generate reusable textures in `src/renderers/textures.ts`; scene-sized
   procedural Battle scenery belongs in `battleBackdrop.ts`. Synthesize audio
   in `src/systems/audio.ts`; do not add external assets.
4. Preserve shared scene state across transitions.
5. Use `debugLog()` and debug-panel APIs instead of `console.log`.
6. Add deterministic Vitest coverage for game logic.

## Current architecture

- Phaser 4 scenes: `Boot`, `Overworld`, `Battle`, `Shop`, `Codex`, `Cutscene`,
  `Ending`, and `Defeat`
- Overworld orchestration: `src/scenes/Overworld.ts`
- Battle orchestration: `src/scenes/Battle.ts`
- Core mechanics: `src/systems/`
- Immutable definitions: `src/data/`
- Extracted presentation: `src/renderers/`
- Battle environment composition: `src/renderers/battleBackdrop.ts`
- Shared Battle depth contract: `src/renderers/battleDepth.ts`
- Stateful scene helpers: `src/managers/`
- Shared audio/accessibility preferences: `src/systems/accessibility.ts`
- Typed semantic actions and state: `src/systems/input.ts`
- Keyboard/pointer/gamepad/touch adapter: `src/managers/input.ts`

The versioned `2dnd_preferences` document is separate from campaign saves and
backs both title and in-game settings. Install the scene accessibility adapter
in every scene, use its shared reduced-motion accessors, preserve
100%/125%/150% text usability, and pair important color states with a textual or
symbolic cue. Control presentation preferences cover touch visibility,
handedness, and prompt source without changing campaign saves. Stable mappings
are intentionally not remappable.

All release input routes through the semantic action layer. Standard gamepads
use dead zones, digital fallback, repeat/debounce, source switching, and a
visible right-stick cursor clicked by pressing the stick. Responsive touch controls use safe areas, pointer
capture for held directions, click pulses for discrete actions, and mobile text
entry. Clear held state on blur, visibility loss, disconnect, scene changes,
and shutdown.

Cutscene contracts live in `src/data/cutsceneTypes.ts`, focused campaign and
boss definitions live in `cutsceneCampaign.ts` and `cutsceneBosses.ts`, and
`src/data/cutscenes.ts` is the stable-ID hub. Pure trigger snapshots, priority
ordering, queue lifecycle, recovery, Chronicle selection, and summary logic live
in `src/systems/cutscenes.ts`; `src/managers/cutscene.ts` owns step progression;
scenes and renderers own input and presentation.
Hero-role actors remain immutable staging cues and resolve at presentation time
from the current `PlayerState`. Build the canonical descriptor with
`src/systems/heroVisuals.ts` and acquire cleanup-safe procedural textures through
`src/renderers/heroTextures.ts`; do not duplicate class, appearance, equipment
layer, fallback, or cache-key rules in Cutscene, Overworld, Battle, or Ending.
`EndingScene` and `DefeatScene` share `src/renderers/result.ts`; defeat receives
an exact runtime-only `PartyDefeatResult`, while the recovered player state is
autosaved before presentation.

The map hub is `src/data/map.ts`; terrain/types, chunks, cities, and dungeons
are split into dedicated modules. Dungeon trap definitions live in
`src/data/traps.ts`, mechanics in `src/systems/traps.ts`, and scene orchestration
in `src/managers/dungeonTraps.ts`.
Group templates live in `src/data/monsterGroups.ts`; reusable initiative,
formation, synergy, reward, and per-combatant rules live in
`src/systems/groupCombat.ts`.
That module also owns party-ready `BattleCombatantState`, stable actor IDs,
actor-ID initiative, ally/enemy targeting, monster party-target selection, and
battle resolution hooks.
`src/systems/battleActions.ts` is the Phaser-free action planner for player
input and ranked gambits: actor enumeration, target binding, validation,
immutable plans, per-actor action/bonus consumption, and one-action dispatch.
`executeValidatedBattleAction()` binds a generic `CombatActorState` to a party
combatant and reuses existing attack, spell, ability, item, defend, element,
status, MP, and inventory mechanics.
Consumables consume the acting source's inventory while applying HP/MP/cures
to a selected ally source; execution contexts must include all party action
sources. Equipment actions remain self-targeted.

`src/systems/animation.ts` is the Phaser-free presentation contract for actor
states, deterministic timing, stable-ID target mapping, once-only lifecycle,
and explicit family/frame texture metadata. `src/managers/actorAnimation.ts`
owns reusable Phaser poses and cleanup; battle/world directors consume resolved
state without changing mechanics. `src/renderers/actorTextures.ts` supports
optional family frames from #49 and a generic existing-texture fallback.

Tutorial and Tips content lives in `src/data/tutorial.ts` as immutable steps,
semantic control actions, categories, and unlock requirements.
`src/systems/tutorial.ts` owns completion normalization and progression-aware
filtering. `src/managers/tutorial.ts` owns the Overworld overlay and renders prompts for
the active keyboard, pointer, gamepad, or touch source. New saves persist
`player.progression.tutorial.completed`; replay never resets it.

Progressive feature discovery is data-driven through
`src/data/featureDiscovery.ts` and `src/systems/featureDiscovery.ts`. Filter
menus, tabs, shortcuts, prompts, touch actions, and Codex/crafting/gathering
categories through the shared registry. Preserve always-safe Inventory, Map,
Equipment, Tips, Settings, and save/title controls, and never use discovery as
authority for gameplay state.

World Event content lives in `src/data/worldEvents.ts`, its deterministic
Phaser-free state machine in `src/systems/worldEvents.ts`, and accessible choice
presentation in `src/managers/worldEvents.ts`. Events short-circuit treasure,
exploration checks, and random encounters for their movement step, while
transitions, entrances, traps, interactions, and queued cutscenes retain
priority. Special event combats use normal Battle hooks and saves.

## Quests

- Put quest definitions, stage objectives, NPC IDs, rewards, and gated
  entrances in `src/data/quests.ts`.
- Put progression, normalization, idempotent rewards, NPC interaction
  resolution, journal entries, and entrance checks behind
  `src/systems/quests.ts`; `questState.ts` and `questDebug.ts` contain focused
  normalization and debug-only mutation helpers.
- Persist state only through `player.progression.quests`; use quest-system APIs
  instead of direct mutation.
- The shipped campaign is the seven-chapter Twelvefold Covenant across all 12
  cities and three keystones, with Ironbound Dispatch, Silk Against the Cold,
  and optional Hydra and Dragon objectives.
- Persist objective counters and claimed reward IDs. Batch group defeats with
  duplicate monster IDs intact so three matching combatants count as three.
- Downstream unlocks such as companions should call `isQuestCompleted()` and
  keep their own persistent state separate from quest reward bookkeeping.
- Cross-system outcomes use stable quest completion actions with
  `{ id, type, targetId }`. Replay them after load/mutations and make the
  consumer idempotent rather than adding duplicate quest state.
- Give every stage a stable camelCase `id`; downstream systems use
  `getQuestStageIndex()` or the debug-only `setQuestStageById()`, never display
  titles.
- Derive boss objectives from `defeatedBosses` so older saves can report
  already-completed objectives.
- Keep quest NPCs available at night and test every referenced NPC, boss,
  reward item, and entrance.
- Campaign completion remains derived from the main quest. Launch the epilogue
  after the final Elowen dialogue applies rewards, recover completed-but-unseen
  saves from Overworld creation, and keep replay presentation-only.
- Queue stable cutscene IDs and save before presentation. Completion or skip
  moves an ID from `pendingCutsceneIds` to `seenCutsceneIds`; reload resumes the
  first pending entry, while Chronicle replay changes neither collection.
- Detect newly satisfied cutscenes by comparing immutable before/after snapshots.
  Battle must capture its snapshot before recording the defeated boss. Sort
  simultaneous triggers by explicit numeric priority rather than discovery
  order.
- Map main-quest talk objectives through `QUEST_NPCS` and assert exact coverage
  of all 12 live city IDs; do not accept name-only references.
- Canyonwatch, Ashfall, and the Volcanic Forge are hard gates. Sandport and
  Heartlands Crypt remain open; other premature travel uses one-time soft
  danger warnings and capped encounter modifiers.

## Non-combat skill checks

Non-combat checks are split across:

- `src/data/skillChecks.ts`: NPC challenges, negotiation choices, and terrain
  event definitions
- `src/systems/skillChecks.ts`: pure d20 resolution, normalization, and helpers
- `src/managers/skillChecks.ts`: Overworld rewards, hazards, chest checks, and
  dialogue orchestration

## Adding monsters

1. Define the monster in the appropriate focused pool (`monsters.ts`,
   `nightMonsters.ts`, or `monsterVariants.ts`).
2. Use a camelCase ID and set a valid typed `family`, stats, rewards, drops,
   abilities, and `isBoss`.
3. For a palette/stat variant, set `variantOf` to a valid same-family monster,
   use a distinct color and ability set, and assign a positive
   `encounterWeight`.
4. Add an `affinity` and `elementalProfile` when the monster has a dominant
   element, resistances, weaknesses, or
   immunities.
5. Add `element` and `statusEffect` to monster abilities when applicable.
6. Ensure the definition is included in `ALL_MONSTERS`; debug spawning, Codex
   browsing, and ID lookup depend on the master list.
7. Reuse `getMonsterTextureKey()` and the family silhouette renderer rather than
   adding scene-local textures or tints.
8. Add encounter-pool, family, palette, texture-key, and data-integrity tests.

Use `getMonster(id)` for exact ID lookup and `findMonster(query)` for
case-insensitive ID/name lookup with partial matching.

## Adding monster groups

1. Add a 2-4 member template to `MONSTER_GROUP_TEMPLATES`.
2. Reference valid monster IDs and assign every member to `front` or `back`.
3. Keep `minPlayerLevel` high enough that total difficulty does not exceed
   `playerLevel * 3`.
4. Add biome/dungeon tags, encounter weight, and an optional synergy with a
   valid break threshold.
5. Add deterministic generation and data-integrity coverage.

Random groups start at level 2, cap at 50% of triggered encounters, and never
replace bosses or explicit debug monster spawns.

Codex family completion is derived from the current `CodexData.entries`; family
metadata, affinity, and sort/filter presentation are not save fields.

World knowledge definitions live in `src/data/codexKnowledge.ts`. Persist only
stable unlocked knowledge IDs in `CodexData`; derive category counts, source
hints, search results, sorting, and grouping from canonical entries. Emit
idempotent location, quest, cutscene, item, NPC, readable, or `worldEvent`
signals without letting Codex state control gameplay. `reputationMilestone`
is owned by the schema-v12 reputation system and must remain idempotent.

## World Events

- Filter immutable definitions by terrain, area, time, weather, level, quest
  state, boss state, prior outcomes, repeat limits, and cooldowns.
- Keep event chance independently capped at 8%; never feed it into or multiply
  the 15% random-encounter calculation.
- Persist the selected pending event before presenting choices or starting a
  special battle. Reload resumes the same choice or encounter.
- Apply skill outcomes through `rollSkillCheck()`, quest starts through
  `startQuestById()`, rewards through canonical item/XP helpers, and lore through
  `unlockCodexFromFutureSignal()`.
- Resolve stable outcome/reward IDs once, append at most 40 chronological
  records, and expose those records through Chronicle without revealing future
  choices.
- Alignment/reputation hooks are consumed by the centralized social mutation
  API with stable source IDs. World Event state never persists duplicate social
  scores or applied IDs.

## Alignment and reputation

- Keep canonical axes, faction IDs, reputation tiers, and thresholds in
  `src/data/reputation.ts`; reusable mechanics belong in
  `src/systems/reputation.ts`.
- New players begin exactly Chaotic Neutral (`lawChaos: -50`, `goodEvil: 0`).
- Persist only bounded scores, stable applied source IDs, and the bounded
  recent-cause history. Derive names, tiers, pricing, milestones, and ending
  variants.
- Apply social outcomes only for meaningful choices. Never reward routine
  movement, unavoidable combat, or farming.
- Return runtime-only `SocialAchievementHook` values for the achievement
  consumer; do not persist achievements inside the social system.

## Achievements

- Put immutable definitions and cosmetic titles in `src/data/achievements.ts`;
  put normalization, deterministic progress, reconciliation, stable event
  counters, debug exclusion, and title equip rules in
  `src/systems/achievements.ts`.
- Prefer reconciliation from authoritative quest, boss, Codex, exploration,
  trap, skill-check, event, social, party, and inventory state. Add persisted
  counters only for non-reconstructable event history such as battle wins,
  one-hit defeats, and explicit defeat count.
- Achievement state never controls gameplay authority. Titles are
  presentation-only and notices are queued for safe Overworld presentation.

## Adding spells, abilities, and equipment

- Damage sources may declare an `Element` from `src/data/elements.ts`.
- Player abilities may apply `selfEffect` or `targetEffect` IDs defined by
  `src/systems/statusEffects.ts`.
- Monster abilities use `statusEffect` for effects applied to the player.
- Cure consumables declare matching cure data and must be wired through
  `useItem()` without consuming the item when no matching ailment exists.
- Ally-target consumables declare `targetType`; resolve it through
  `getItemTargetType()` so older inventory copies use canonical item metadata.
- Preserve action economy: normal actions end the player turn; bonus-action
  abilities and the first item use do not.

Combat calculation order is:

1. Roll and resolve the attack or save.
2. Apply active-status accuracy, disadvantage, AC, and damage modifiers.
3. Apply elemental immunity, weakness, or resistance to the modified damage.
4. Apply damage and status effects.
5. Report discoveries and combat feedback.

Magic Missile remains auto-hit and does not roll disadvantage.

## Status effects

All definitions and lifecycle helpers live in
`src/systems/statusEffects.ts`. Do not duplicate status logic in data files or
scenes.

- Start of actor turn: tick damage, saving throws, and skip-turn decision.
- End of actor turn: decrement durations and expire effects.
- Apply or refresh through `applyStatusEffect()`.
- Normalize loaded effects through `normalizeActiveEffects()`.
- Clear player and monster effects when leaving Battle; durations are measured
  in combat turns, not overworld steps.

## Elements

Supported elements are Fire, Ice, Lightning, Poison, Necrotic, Radiant,
Thunder, Force, and Psychic.

- Immunity: zero damage
- Weakness: double damage
- Resistance: floor of half damage
- Neutral: unchanged

Record observed non-neutral interactions with `discoverElement()` so the Codex
can persist and display them.

## World features

- Cities may contain connected districts. Always use city chunk helpers rather
  than indexing `city.chunks` directly.
- Dungeons may contain multiple levels. Always use dungeon level and
  connection helpers.
- Dungeon trap layouts are derived from persisted `trapSeed`; never mutate
  dungeon maps or randomize layouts independently in scenes.
- Detected traps block movement until disarmed. Trap triggers must short-circuit
  the normal random-encounter check for that step.
- Use `FogOfWar.exploredKey()` for exploration keys.
- Use `isWalkable()` and `ENCOUNTER_RATES`; do not hardcode terrain behavior.
- Nautical metadata lives in `src/data/nautical.ts`; state normalization,
  ownership, and mechanics live in the focused `nauticalState.ts`,
  `nauticalOwnership.ts`, and `nautical.ts` modules. Preserve all 90 legacy
  chunk IDs and use `s:zoneId,chunkX,chunkY,x,y` for sea fog.
- Merchant routes work before boat ownership. Free sailing requires a
  serviceable active boat, uses canonical Water eligibility, and runs hazards
  before World Events, gathering, and random sea encounters.

## Non-combat skill checks

- Checks use d20 + Dexterity, Intelligence, Wisdom, or Charisma modifier plus
  typed bonuses against a DC.
- Natural 1 and 20 are not automatic outcomes for ability checks.
- Persist fixed NPC, shop, chest, and treasure results in
  `player.progression.skillChecks`.
- Use stable NPC identities and shop type/coordinate keys rather than array
  indexes.
- Shop negotiation is one attempt per shop; successful discounts restore from
  the saved result.
- Exploration hazard damage is nonlethal and must clamp the player to at least
  1 HP.
- Test roll math, invalid inputs, stable data references, save normalization,
  reward bounds, and nonlethal damage deterministically.

## Scene changes

State-bearing transitions commonly pass:

```typescript
{
  player,
  defeatedBosses,
  codex,
  timeStep,
  weatherState,
  savedSpecialNpcs,
}
```

Battle also receives a `MonsterEncounter` and biome; Shop receives shop/city
context.
Defeat receives the full shared state plus encounter name/type and the exact
applied party defeat receipt. It must not recalculate or reapply penalties.
Future party systems pass accessor-backed `partyCombatants` plus runtime-only
`battleHooks`; do not persist those wrapper objects.
Keep target `init()` contracts and every caller synchronized.

The new-player tutorial opens only after pending opening cutscenes have drained.
`F1` and the Esc menu open the consultable Tips surface. Keep the external HTML
control rail collapsed by default and retain only contextual action prompts in
the game HUD.

Route camera fades and scene handoffs through
`src/managers/sceneTransition.ts`. Call `prepare()` when each scene creates,
wait for fade-complete events, and keep the duration-plus-grace watchdog as a
recovery path only. Restore the outgoing camera before queueing the next scene,
reject duplicate handoffs, and block state-changing Overworld input until the
queued start/restart is processed. Every Overworld restart must include a fresh
`savedSpecialNpcs` snapshot in the shared state payload.
Use the same guarded Battle exit cleanup for victory, flee, and defeat. Defeat
clears transient menus, input, effects, particles, and weather timers before
starting `DefeatScene`, which continues only to Overworld.
- Resolve an action before presenting it. Actor animation may read stable IDs,
  targets, hit/damage/healing, and outcome, but must not spend MP/items/actions,
  apply damage, report results, or control fade-complete scene handoffs.

## Companions and gambits

- Persistent party state lives at `player.party`; do not add a parallel scene
  payload or companion combat model.
- Stable companion IDs are `guardian`, `scout`, and `mystic`.
- Build runtime actors with `createPartyCombatant()` and
  `createBattleActionSource()`.
- Manual turns and ranked gambits both validate/execute through
  `battleActions.ts`; one bonus action may precede or follow one main action.
- Recruitment consumes replayable quest completion actions idempotently.
- Debug quest or companion recruitment must refresh live follower presentation
  immediately after replay.
- Active conscious companions may render as non-blocking followers, but only
  hero movement invokes trap, encounter, gate, and world-interaction logic.
- Keep party UI/followers/battle presentation in focused managers/renderers
  rather than growing the existing oversized scene/overlay files.

## Inventory presentation

- Build immutable views with `src/systems/inventory.ts`; every view entry keeps
  its original inventory index for actions and transfers.
- Never sort the owning inventory array or replace equipment object references.
- Keep sort/filter/search preferences in `2dnd_inventory_prefs`, outside the
  campaign save schema. Recent acquisition is reverse append order.
- Use semantic inventory actions for keyboard, pointer, gamepad, and touch
  controls. `T` remains mount control.
- Generate item visuals procedurally through `src/renderers/itemVisuals.ts`.

## Gathering

Gathering content lives in `src/data/gathering.ts`, deterministic node/table/
minigame logic in `src/systems/gathering.ts`, schema normalization in
`gatheringState.ts`, and accessible Phaser presentation in
`src/managers/gathering.ts`. Persist selected outcomes before play, use safe
location-derived nodes, route guarded finds through normal Battle hooks, and
keep material identity limited to stable `Item.material` recipe-input metadata.

## Crafting

Crafting recipes live in `src/data/crafting.ts`, atomic mechanics and discovery
in `src/systems/crafting.ts`, persistence normalization in `craftingState.ts`,
and accessible Overworld presentation in `src/managers/crafting.ts`. Validate
the selected actor inventory, protected/equipped restrictions, batch, gold,
station, output, and transaction ID before mutation. Equipment upgrades replace
exact equipped object links with canonical outputs. Never pull companion
materials implicitly, reroll a craft, duplicate material identity, or let
recipes/achievements control quests, Codex, access, or rewards.

## Validation

```bash
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run test:browser
npm run build
```

For UI changes, run the committed Playwright flow in headless Chromium. Keep
browser actions synchronized through debug-state transitions, and hold
frame-polled Phaser keys across frames rather than using instantaneous presses.
Build responsive UI from `src/systems/layout.ts`, register modal groups through
`createOverlayContainer()`, and assert the local `#layout-report` reports zero
unintended overlap or clipping at supported text scales.

## Common pitfalls

- Do not mutate shared monster, item, map, city, or dungeon definitions.
- Do not share HP, status, defend, discovery, or drop state between group
  combatants, including duplicate monsters.
- Do not introduce index-based turn entries or duplicate hero HP/effect state;
  use stable combatant IDs and `createHeroCombatant()`.
- Do not reimplement MP, inventory, target, formation, or action-economy checks
  in companion AI; use `validateBattleAction()`.
- Do not use stale Phaser 3 APIs or default imports; current code uses
  `import * as Phaser from "phaser"`.
- Do not create a second status or elemental calculation path.
- Do not omit unique dungeon pools or bosses from aggregate lookups.
- Do not use geometry masks for the Battle log; render the bounded visible
  message window.
- Do not add a persistent field without save normalization and tests.
- Do not reroll a failed trap detection; persist the `missed` state.

1. # 2D&D
2. 
3. A browser-based JRPG that combines Dragon Quest-style exploration with
4. Dungeons & Dragons 5E-inspired combat. The game runs entirely in the browser:
5. graphics are procedurally generated, audio is synthesized with the Web Audio
6. API, and saves use `localStorage`.
7. 
8. ## Features
9. 
10. ### Character creation and progression
11. 
12. - 12 classes: Knight, Ranger, Wizard, Sorcerer, Rogue, Paladin, Warlock,
13.   Cleric, Druid, Barbarian, Monk, and Bard
14. - D&D 5E point buy: 27 points, base scores from 8 to 15
15. - Optional 4d6-drop-lowest random stat generation
16. - Class ability boosts, class-specific primary stats, spells, martial
17.   abilities, talents, equipment, shields, mounts, and banking
18. - Leveling to 20 with hit-die HP growth, proficiency bonuses, and ability score
19.   improvements
20. - Three quest-recruited companions (Guardian, Scout, Mystic) with independent
21.   levels, stats, HP/MP, spells, abilities, equipment, inventories, and ASI
22.   progression
23. - Hero plus three active companions, reserve/active ordering, item transfers,
24.   party-wide inn recovery, and persistent manual or gambit control
25. - Large hero and companion inventories support immutable sorting by type,
26.   value, rarity, recent acquisition, or name; category filters, search,
27.   generated item visuals, and stable keyboard, pointer, gamepad, and touch
28.   selection
29. - Ranked 12-rule gambits use structured subjects, conditions, actions, and
30.   targets; invalid rules safely fall through without consuming resources
31. 
32. ### Combat
33. 
34. - Turn-based d20 combat with initiative, natural 1/20 outcomes, critical hits,
35.   defending, fleeing, off-hand attacks, spells, abilities, consumables, and
36.   boss abilities
37. - Balanced encounters with 1-4 monsters, individual initiative turns,
38.   front/back formations, semantic keyboard, pointer, gamepad, or touch target
39.   selection, and group
40.   synergies such as Pack Tactics, Shield Wall, War Cry, healer support, and
41.   elemental combos
42. - Party battles use stable combatant IDs, explicit party/enemy allegiance,
43.   individual initiative, ally/enemy target scopes, living-party monster target
44.   selection, manual companion turns, automated gambits, and shared result hooks
45. - `battleActions.ts` provides a Phaser-free gambit pipeline to enumerate living
46.   actors, bind matched and item-declared ally/self targets, validate
47.   MP/inventory/action economy, freeze an action plan, consume one action plus
48.   one bonus action per actor, and dispatch one attack, defend, spell, ability,
49.   or item action
50. - Generic `BattleActionSource` and `executeValidatedBattleAction()` reuse the
51.   game's d20, AC, elements, statuses, MP, inventory, healing, and defend rules
52.   for player or future companion actors
53. - Battle consumables use item-declared target scopes: ally items fall back to
54.   self when solo, self-only items remain self, and the acting actor consumes
55.   the item while HP, MP, or cures apply to the selected target
56. - Single-target, row-targeted, random-two, and all-enemy spell targeting; AoE
57.   spells pay MP and roll damage once, then resolve each monster independently
58. - Single/all-party healing, Mass Haste, and Inspiring Chorus apply one shared
59.   roll/cost across the resolved party targets
60. - Nine damage elements: Fire, Ice, Lightning, Poison, Necrotic, Radiant,
61.   Thunder, Force, and Psychic
62. - Monster weaknesses deal double damage, resistances halve damage, and
63.   immunities prevent damage
64. - Elemental interactions are discovered through combat and recorded per
65.   monster in the Codex
66. - Every monster belongs to one of 14 typed families with a stable base/variant
67.   relationship, weighted encounter eligibility, and a family-specific
68.   procedural silhouette. Palette variants keep distinct abilities, drops,
69.   elemental profiles, and difficulty, while bosses use richer family forms.
70. - The typed Codex preserves monster defeat, AC, elemental, drop, family, and
71.   completion discovery while adding locations, items, characters, factions,
72.   and history from canonical campaign data.
73. - Knowledge unlocks are idempotent and source-driven through city/dungeon
74.   exploration, quest stages/completions, cutscenes, item acquisition, named NPC
75.   dialogue, and readable statues or temple records. Lore never controls quests,
76.   rewards, companions, gates, or outcomes.
77. - Category filters, search, canonical/name/source sorting, discovered grouping,
78.   source hints, and non-blocking discovery notices support keyboard, pointer,
79.   touch, gamepad cursor, 150% text, high contrast, and reduced motion.
80. - 15 status effects shared by players and monsters:
81.   Poisoned, Burning, Frozen, Paralyzed, Stunned, Frightened, Slowed, Prone,
82.   Asleep, Confused, Enraged, Hasted, Inspired, Raging, and Sneak Stance
83. - Start-of-turn damage and saving throws, skipped turns, attack disadvantage,
84.   accuracy/AC/damage modifiers, duration expiration, and cure items
85. - Combat effects are cleared when Battle ends because their durations use the
86.   combat turn clock
87. - Full-party defeat opens a dedicated procedural result sequence for random and
88.   boss encounters, lists every defeated actor, reports the exact gold and XP
89.   losses, autosaves the recovered state, and continues from the last town with
90.   half HP/MP and no battle effects or overlapping weather ambience
91. - Stable-ID battle presentation animates hero, companion, monster, and boss
92.   idle, attack, cast, ability, item, defend, damage, victory, faint, and flee
93.   states after mechanics resolve, without changing action economy or outcomes
94. 
95. ### Non-combat skill checks
96. 
97. - D20 ability checks use the player's Dexterity, Intelligence, Wisdom, or
98.   Charisma modifier;
99.   natural 1 and 20 are not automatic outcomes outside attack rolls
100. - Charisma supports persistent Persuade/Bluff NPC outcomes and one-attempt shop
101.   negotiations with 10% or 20% discounts
102. - Wisdom uncovers hidden trails, dungeon passages, secret chest compartments,
103.   and better rewards from overworld treasure
104. - Dexterity avoids exploration hazards and resolves locked or trapped chests;
105.   failed hazards can cost HP but cannot defeat the player outside combat
106. - Fixed checks use stable save IDs, while repeatable terrain events remain
107.   data-driven by environment and terrain
108. 
109. ### World exploration
110. 
111. - A 10x9 world grid containing 90 chunks, each 20x15 tiles
112. - Four named landmasses—Frostcrown, Verdant Covenant, Ember March, and
113.   Southreach—assigned over the unchanged 90 legacy chunk identities, with five
114.   navigable sea zones and compatible overworld fog coordinates
115. - Discoverable ports and merchant routes support paid passage before boat
116.   ownership; The Tideglass Charter grants a Reed Skiff and unlocks free sailing,
117.   safe contextual embark/disembark, boat condition, upgrades, and cosmetics
118. - Tidehaven island adds a two-district town, harbor shops and inn, sea materials,
119.   a multi-level trapped grotto, and the optional Deepwake Kraken boss
120. - Sailing alone enables capped sea encounters, day/night sea pools, weather
121.   hazards, open-sea fishing, synthesized wake/audio, and procedural boat art
122. - Distinct terrain, biome encounter tables, night encounters, weather,
123.   day/night lighting, fog of war, treasure, NPCs, animals, and special NPCs
124. - Random encounter modifiers stack but the effective chance is capped at 15%;
125.   group encounters begin at level 2 and use level budgets and biome filters
126. - Seeded, data-driven World Events add shrines, ambushes, travelers, discoveries,
127.   weather hazards, and supply finds. Eligibility uses terrain, area, day/night,
128.   weather, level, quest state, prior outcomes, repeat limits, and cooldowns.
129. - Event choices reuse normal skill checks, quest/reward helpers, Codex
130.   `worldEvent` signals, and the standard Battle pipeline. Pending choices and
131.   special combats recover after reload without rerolling or duplicating rewards.
132. - The Chronicle includes a bounded World Events record with source, location,
133.   time, weather, choice, and resolved outcome.
134. - Fishing, mining, and foraging use stable location-derived nodes and distinct
135.   bite/tension, strike/precision, and search/memory minigames. Eligibility uses
136.   canonical terrain, location context, biome, time, weather, and node cooldowns.
137. - Gathering outcomes are selected and saved before play so reload cannot reroll
138.   rewards. Reduced motion replaces animation timing with deliberate steps while
139.   preserving patterns, score thresholds, outcomes, and rewards.
140. - Thirteen canonical fish, ores, gems, herbs, plants, wood, and relic materials
141.   stack through normal inventory semantics, can be sold at bounded values, and
142.   expose stable recipe-input metadata consumed directly by crafting recipes.
143.   Rare guarded finds enter the normal Battle pipeline.
144. - Fourteen data-driven recipes cover healing, cures, travel supplies, trap
145.   tools, deterministic equipment upgrades, and rare elemental gear. Crafting
146.   validates one selected hero or companion inventory, gold, batch size, station,
147.   protected items, outputs, and equipment links before one atomic transaction.
148. - Recipe discovery is idempotent across exploration, cities, quests, gathering,
149.   shops, NPCs, readable lore, Codex knowledge, items, and World Events. Monster
150.   drops, chests, shops, event rewards, and deterministic minor treasures provide
151.   balanced canonical materials without replacing existing rewards.
152. - 13 cities, including the optional island port Tidehaven, with connected districts, district-specific shops, gates,
153.   discovery, fast travel, inns, banks, stables, and city music
154. - Four multi-level dungeons with bidirectional stairs, floor-specific
155.   encounters, chests, fog, procedural traps, and a unique deepest-floor boss
156. - Seeded trap layouts with spike pits, poison darts, falling rocks, alarms,
157.   hidden floors, and dungeon-specific runes; nearby checks use Dexterity or
158.   Intelligence, detected traps can be disarmed for XP, and unresolved traps can
159.   deal HP/MP damage, inflict combat statuses, summon encounters, or drop the
160.   player to a deeper floor
161. - Trap Kits, class talents, and Adventurer guidance improve detection and
162.   disarming; seeded layouts and four-state trap outcomes persist explicitly
163. - The seven-chapter **Twelvefold Covenant** main quest spans all 12 cities and
164.   restores three keystones guarded by dungeon bosses, with two campaign
165.   sidequests, optional boss objectives, named story NPCs, dynamic markers, a
166.   `Q` journal, unique rewards, gated roads, and soft danger zones
167. - Data-driven campaign cutscenes cover the opening, quest stages, city oaths,
168.   companions, dungeon reveals, route openings, keystones, and every boss
169.   introduction and aftermath; queued scenes survive reloads until completed or
170.   skipped, and the Chronicle replays seen scenes without changing game state
171. - The final Elowen turn-in launches a skippable campaign epilogue with rewards,
172.   party and exploration summaries, credits, post-game continuation, and
173.   presentation-only replay from the in-game menu
174. - Alignment uses bounded Law/Chaos and Good/Evil axes. New heroes begin exactly
175.   Chaotic Neutral, while stable named alignments and epilogue legacy text are
176.   derived from deterministic thresholds
177. - Reputation is tracked independently for all 12 towns and canonical factions.
178.   Its named tiers influence NPC reactions, optional World Events, and additive
179.   shop discounts or surcharges without gating campaign completion
180. - Quest, dialogue, World Event, trap, and morally relevant event-combat outcomes
181.   apply through stable idempotent source IDs. The Party Social page shows both
182.   axes, scores, thresholds, standing tiers, and a bounded recent-cause history
183. - 39 data-driven achievements cover campaign chapters, bosses and dungeons,
184.   combat, secrets, exploration, Codex families, companions and gambits, gathering, World
185.   Events, social milestones, and meaningful equipment collection. Progress is
186.   derived from authoritative game state where possible; one-shot battle history
187.   uses stable once-only counters. Optional title rewards are cosmetic only.
188. - Three additional recruitment quest lines use stable stage IDs and replayable
189.   completion actions; active conscious companions follow the hero and can be
190.   spoken to during overworld, city, and dungeon exploration
191. - Fog keys separate every dungeon level and city district while preserving
192.   legacy level-zero/chunk-zero save keys
193. 
194. ### Presentation
195. 
196. - Phaser 4 pixel-art rendering with procedural textures
197. - Every campaign, optional-boss, Kraken, Chronicle, recovery, and epilogue
198.   cutscene resolves the hero from the current `PlayerState`, including class
199.   build, custom skin/hair colors, armor, main/off-hand weapons, and shields
200. - Animated overworld walking, followers, mount gait, battle actions, boss

162. ## TypeScript and style
163. 
164. - Use strict TypeScript and explicit parameter/return types.
165. - Prefer interfaces for object shapes; use type aliases for unions and
166.   intersections.
167. - Use `import type` for type-only imports.
168. - Prefer `const`, optional chaining, and nullish coalescing.
169. - Do not use `any`; use proper types, guards, or `unknown`.
170. - Use 2-space indentation and reasonable line lengths.
171. - Use camelCase for files in systems/data and PascalCase for scene files.
172. - Use camelCase for values/functions/entity IDs, PascalCase for types, and
173.   UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants.
174. - Add JSDoc for public APIs or non-obvious mechanics; avoid redundant comments.
175. - Keep imports ordered external, internal, then type-only where practical.
176. - Reuse existing helpers before adding parallel logic.
177. 
178. ## Phaser 4 patterns
179. 
180. - Import Phaser with `import * as Phaser from "phaser"`.
181. - Scene keys are `BootScene`, `OverworldScene`, `BattleScene`, `ShopScene`,
182.   `CodexScene`, `CutsceneScene`, `EndingScene`, and `DefeatScene`.
183. - Store scene input in `init()` and reset scene-specific transient state there.
184. - Build state-bearing transition payloads with `createSharedSceneState()` so
185.   they preserve:
186. 
187. ```typescript
188. {
189.   player,
190.   defeatedBosses,
191.   codex,
192.   timeStep,
193.   weatherState,
194.   savedSpecialNpcs,
195. }
196. ```
197. 
198. - Battle also receives a `MonsterEncounter` and `biome`; Shop receives
199.   shop/city context.
200. - Cutscene receives the full shared state plus a stable `CutsceneId`, replay
201.   mode, return scene, and optional runtime-only quest updates. Ending receives
202.   the full shared state plus the epilogue ID. Continue Post-game returns that
203.   state to Overworld, while Return to Title saves before starting Boot.
204. - Defeat receives the full shared state plus the encounter name/type and an
205.   exact runtime-only `PartyDefeatResult`. It never reapplies the penalty and
206.   only offers continuation through the existing town recovery state.
207. - Battle may also receive accessor-backed `partyCombatants` and runtime-only
208.   `battleHooks`; these are scene contracts, not persisted save fields.
209. - Persistent companions live inside `player.party`, so every existing
210.   state-bearing transition carries them through the same `player` object.
211. - Route fades and scene `start()`/`restart()` handoffs through
212.   `SceneTransitionManager`. Restore the outgoing camera before queueing the
213.   next scene, reject duplicate queued handoffs, and call `prepare()` at the
214.   start of every scene `create()`.
215. - Fade-complete events are authoritative. The manager's duration-plus-grace
216.   watchdog is recovery-only; never use an equal-duration timer as the primary
217.   handoff trigger. Remove completed listeners and watchdog timers explicitly.
218. - Phaser scene operations are queued until the next Scene Manager update.
219.   Block state-changing input while a handoff is pending, and keep Overworld
220.   restarts on the shared full-state payload including `savedSpecialNpcs`.
221. - Generate textures through `src/renderers/textures.ts`, invoked by Boot.
222.   Monster silhouettes live in the focused `monsterTextures.ts` renderer.
223. - Resolve hero visuals from live `PlayerState` through
224.   `src/systems/heroVisuals.ts` and lease generated textures through
225.   `src/renderers/heroTextures.ts`. Overworld, Battle, Cutscene, and hero-bearing
226.   Ending steps share this pipeline. Cutscene data stores stable hero roles and
227.   staging only; never store generic hero colors or appearance snapshots.
228. - Battle backdrop geometry is scene-sized procedural rendering owned by
229.   `src/renderers/battleBackdrop.ts`. Use the typed bands in `battleDepth.ts`;
230.   never bake sky and scenery into one opaque layer or introduce scene-local
231.   magic depths.
232. - Keep actor animation contracts in `src/systems/animation.ts`, generic Phaser
233.   pose/tween ownership in `src/managers/actorAnimation.ts`, and scene-specific
234.   orchestration in focused battle/world directors. Presentation reads stable
235.   actor IDs and resolved outcomes; it never mutates combat or quest state.
236. - Build `ActorTextureFamily` metadata with explicit frame keys. Optional
237.   monster-family art supplies stable `monster-<id>-<normal|boss>-<state>` frames;
238.   existing idle textures retain a transform-based fallback without hardcoded
239.   monster IDs.
240. - Synthesize all audio in `src/systems/audio.ts`.
241. - Store Phaser object references needed for later update/cleanup.
242. - Calculate actual scaled UI bounds to prevent overlap.
243. - Default game zoom is 6.
244. - Do not use geometry masks for the Battle log. Render the bounded visible
245.   message window and scroll by message offset.
246. - Keep Battle ordering as sky/stars/celestial/clouds, distant scenery, ground
247.   and props, actor shadows, back/front actors, action particles, front weather,
248.   UI, then debug/transition overlays. Backdrop cleanup owns its emitters,
249.   lightning timers, inspection labels, and containers.

1. # Companions and Gambits
2. 
3. ## Party model
4. 
5. The persistent party lives at `player.party` in save schema v6:
6. 
7. - `companions`: unique recruited `CompanionState` records
8. - `activeCompanionIds`: up to three recruited IDs in battle/follower order
9. 
10. The hero remains the owner of gold, bank balance, world position, mounts, and
11. world progression. Each companion owns independent XP, level, HP/MP, stats,
12. spells, abilities, talents, inventory, equipment, active effects, dialogue
13. cursor, control mode, and gambits.
14. 
15. The three stable companion IDs are:
16. 
17. | ID | Role | Class |
18. | --- | --- | --- |
19. | `guardian` | Defensive frontline | Paladin |
20. | `scout` | Mobile ranged damage | Ranger |
21. | `mystic` | Healing and party support | Cleric |
22. 
23. New recruits match the hero's current level using deterministic historical HP
24. and MP growth. Later XP and level-ups are independent.
25. 
26. ## Recruitment
27. 
28. Recruitment uses the canonical quest system:
29. 
30. - `recruitGuardian`
31. - `recruitScout`
32. - `recruitMystic`
33. 
34. Each quest has stable `meet*`, `*Trial`, and `*Oath` stage IDs and emits one
35. completion action:
36. 
37. ```text
38. companion.recruit.guardian
39. companion.recruit.scout
40. companion.recruit.mystic
41. ```
42. 
43. `replayQuestCompletionActions(..., "recruitCompanion")` runs after load,
44. Overworld initialization, NPC quest changes, and debug quest mutations.
45. `recruitCompanion()` is idempotent, so reloads, rewinds, and repeated debug
46. completion cannot duplicate a companion or starter inventory. Debug quest and
47. companion commands refresh the live follower sprites immediately.
48. 
49. ## Party management
50. 
51. Press `P` during exploration to open the party overlay.
52. 
53. The overlay supports:
54. 
55. - active/reserve membership and active order
56. - manual or gambit combat control
57. - member stats, HP/MP/XP, and equipment
58. - independent inventories and item transfer
59. - targeted consumables and healing outside combat
60. - pending companion stat allocation
61. - ranked gambit editing
62. 
63. The Items page uses immutable sorted and filtered views, full-text search,
64. procedural item visuals, and stable keyboard/pointer selection for large bags.
65. Its sort, filter, and search preferences are stored separately from actor
66. ownership. See [`inventory.md`](inventory.md) for controls and selector rules.
67. 
68. Key items, mounts, and equipped items cannot be transferred. Gold remains with
69. the hero; shop purchases and battle drops enter the hero bag and can then be
70. transferred.
71. 
72. ## Gambit rules
73. 
74. Each companion can store up to 12 enabled or disabled rules. Rank 1 has highest
75. priority.
76. 
77. The structured rule format is:
78. 
79. ```text
80. if [subject] has/is [condition] do [action] on [target]
81. ```
82. 
83. Supported subjects include self, hero, any party member, a specific companion,
84. and any enemy. Conditions cover HP/MP values or percentages, statuses,
85. alive/KO state, and ability-score comparisons. Actions cover attack, defend,
86. known spells, known abilities, and owned items. Targets include the matched
87. subject, named party members, lowest/highest HP allies or enemies, and
88. automatic area targets.
89. 
90. At the start of a gambit-controlled turn:
91. 
92. 1. Status start-of-turn processing resolves.
93. 2. Rules are evaluated by ascending rank against a fresh battle snapshot.
94. 3. Invalid targets, missing items, insufficient MP, consumed action slots, and
95.    inapplicable heals/buffs fall through without mutation.
96. 4. A valid bonus action may execute first.
97. 5. Lower-ranked rules continue until one main action executes.
98. 6. If no rule executes, the companion attacks; if no enemy is valid, it
99.    defends.
100. 
101. Manual companion turns and gambits both use `validateBattleAction()` and
102. `executeValidatedBattleAction()`.
103. 
104. ## Battle, KO, and rewards
105. 
106. Every conscious party member rolls initiative. Monsters select only living
107. party actors. Battle ends in defeat only when the whole active party is KO.
108. 
109. Living members receive victory XP. A member knocked out during the battle
110. receives no victory XP and loses progress earned toward the next level, down to
111. the current-level XP floor. A partially victorious KO member remains at 0 HP
112. until an inn.
113. 
114. On a full wipe:
115. 
116. - every active member receives the KO XP penalty
117. - the existing 30% hero-gold penalty applies once
118. - the party returns to the last town
119. - active members recover half HP/MP
120. - Battle effects are cleared and the recovered state is autosaved
121. - `DefeatScene` shows every defeated member, exact gold/XP losses, and the
122.   recovery location before continuing; boss and random encounters share this
123.   path
124. 
125. Inn rest revives and fully restores every recruited companion and processes
126. their pending level-ups.
127. 
128. ## Followers and world integration
129. 
130. Active conscious companions follow the hero using prior valid hero tiles. They
131. do not block movement or independently trigger traps, encounters, gates, or
132. world interactions. Pointer interaction talks directly to a follower; Space
133. uses companion dialogue only after higher-priority world interactions.
134. 
135. Dungeon movement preserves `DungeonTrapManager` ordering:
136. 
137. ```text
138. trap move/arrival handling -> exploration event -> random encounter
139. ```
140. 
141. Companions travel inside the existing `player` scene payload, so Battle, Shop,
142. Codex, fast travel, alarm encounters, and scene restarts preserve one party
143. state without a parallel transition field.
144. 
145. ## Debug commands
146. 
147. ```text
148. /companion list
149. /companion recruit <guardian|scout|mystic|all>
150. /companion mode <id> <manual|gambit>
151. /companion heal
152. /companion gambits <id>
153. ```
154. 
155. The debug MP hotkey is `O`; `P` is reserved for party management.
156.

344. `map.ts` is the map hub. Core types and dimensions live in `mapTypes.ts`;
345. world chunks, cities, and dungeons live in their own data modules. Overworld
346. delegates rendering and stateful subsystems to `renderers/` and `managers/`.
347. 
348. Tutorial steps, semantic control guidance, tips, categories, and unlock
349. requirements live in `src/data/tutorial.ts`. `src/systems/tutorial.ts` owns
350. Phaser-free completion normalization and progression-aware filtering, while
351. `src/managers/tutorial.ts` owns the adaptive overlay. Completion
352. persists at `player.progression.tutorial`; the compact HTML control rail starts
353. collapsed now that equivalent guidance is available from the game.
354. 
355. `src/systems/input.ts` defines stable semantic actions, contexts, standard
356. keyboard/gamepad mappings, dead-zone normalization, source switching,
357. repeat/debounce, context priority, and duplicate-action suppression.
358. `src/managers/input.ts` is the single browser/Phaser adapter for keyboard,
359. pointer, standard gamepads, and responsive touch controls. It clears held state
360. on blur, visibility loss, disconnection, and scene changes; exposes the active
361. source on the canvas; and provides a visible right-stick gamepad cursor for
362. pointer-first surfaces.
363. 
364. Quest content lives in `src/data/quests.ts`; runtime progression, rewards, NPC
365. interactions, journal entries, access rules, danger states, and completion
366. actions go through `src/systems/quests.ts`. Save normalization is isolated in
367. `src/systems/questState.ts`, debug-only mutation in
368. `src/systems/questDebug.ts`, and Overworld presentation flow in
369. `src/managers/questFlow.ts`. Add content through these APIs rather than
370. mutating `player.progression.quests` directly. Systems such as companion
371. recruitment should query `isQuestCompleted()` and persist their own state.
372. Completed quests may also declare stable `{ id, type, targetId }` actions.
373. Consumers call `getQuestCompletionActions()` or
374. `replayQuestCompletionActions()` after load and quest mutations, then apply
375. those actions idempotently in their own state. Every stage also has a stable
376. data ID; use `getQuestStageIndex()` or the debug-only
377. `setQuestStageById()` helper instead of coupling systems to display text.
378. 
379. Cutscene contracts live in `src/data/cutsceneTypes.ts`; campaign and boss content
380. live in focused modules, and `src/data/cutscenes.ts` remains the stable-ID hub.
381. `src/systems/cutscenes.ts` owns trigger snapshots, deterministic queue order,
382. normalization, lifecycle, Chronicle selection, and legacy epilogue recovery.
383. `src/managers/cutscene.ts` advances or skips immutable steps.
384. `CutsceneScene` and `src/renderers/cutscene.ts` provide procedural presentation.
385. Hero-role actors are runtime-resolved through the canonical descriptor in
386. `src/systems/heroVisuals.ts` and leased procedural textures in
387. `src/renderers/heroTextures.ts`; immutable cutscene data stores staging roles,
388. not appearance snapshots. The same pipeline supplies Overworld, Battle, and
389. hero-bearing Ending steps, with stable keys covering every visible input and
390. safe category fallbacks for equipment without a dedicated family. Debug mode
391. provides `/cutsceneview <id> <fixture> <loadout>` plus an inspection report.
392. `EndingScene` and `DefeatScene` share
393. `src/renderers/result.ts` for campaign-summary, credits, and defeat-result
394. surfaces. IDs are queued and saved before presentation, then removed from
395. `pendingCutsceneIds` and added to `seenCutsceneIds` only after completion or
396. skip. Chronicle replay changes neither list.
397. 
398. `src/systems/animation.ts` defines Phaser-free actor states, deterministic
399. reduced-motion timing, stable-ID target mapping, once-only lifecycle gates, and
400. the family/frame texture contract. `src/managers/actorAnimation.ts` owns generic
401. pose/tween cleanup, while battle and world directors orchestrate feedback
402. without delaying authoritative turn, result, or scene-transition state.
403. `src/renderers/actorTextures.ts` consumes optional family metadata from #49 and
404. falls back to current procedural textures when family frames are unavailable.
405. `src/renderers/battleBackdrop.ts` owns Battle's procedural sky, celestial,
406. scenery, ground, prop, shadow, and split weather layers. The typed global order
407. is centralized in `src/renderers/battleDepth.ts`, keeping world layers below
408. actors/effects and all of them below Battle UI and camera transitions.
409. 
410. For companion recruitment, define three distinct quest IDs and one action per
411. path using `type: "recruitCompanion"` and the companion ID as `targetId`.
412. `recruitCompanion()` must keep recruited IDs unique, so reloads, debug quest
413. completion, and replay cannot duplicate a companion. Debug quest and companion
414. mutations also refresh live followers immediately.
415. 
416. `SceneTransitionManager` owns camera fades and scene handoffs. It resets stale
417. effects on scene entry, waits for Phaser's fade-complete event, restores the
418. outgoing camera before queueing the next scene, rejects duplicate handoffs, and
419. uses a delayed watchdog only to recover a missing event. Overworld restarts
420. share one complete player, party, world, quest, trap, weather, and NPC payload
421. and block state-changing input until Phaser processes the queued handoff.
422. Battle uses the same guarded handoff for victory, flee, and defeat. Defeat first
423. creates an exact `PartyDefeatResult`, saves the recovered player, clears
424. transient battle input/effects/weather, then starts `DefeatScene`; continuing
425. returns the complete shared state to Overworld without applying the penalty
426. again.
427. 
428. See [`docs/companions.md`](docs/companions.md) for party state, recruitment,
429. inventories, gambit syntax, combat control, KO/reward rules, and debug commands.
430. See [`docs/inventory.md`](docs/inventory.md) for immutable inventory views,
431. presentation preferences, controls, generated visuals, and transfer restrictions.

433. ## Getting started
434. 
435. ```bash
436. git clone https://github.com/mbianchidev/2dnd.git
437. cd 2dnd
438. npm install
439. npm run test:browser:install
440. npm run dev
441. ```
442. 
443. Vite serves the game at `http://localhost:3000`.
444. 
445. ## Commands
446. 
447. ```bash
448. npm run dev        # Start the Vite development server
449. npm run typecheck  # Run strict TypeScript checks
450. npm test           # Run the Vitest suite once
451. npm run test:browser # Run the headless Chromium campaign golden path
452. npm run test:watch # Run Vitest in watch mode
453. npm run build      # Type-check and create a production build
454. ```
